In [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), especially in the study of [dynamical systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamical_system), a **limit set** is the state a dynamical system reaches after an infinite amount of time has passed, by either going forward or backwards in time. Limit sets are important because they can be used to understand the long term behavior of a dynamical system. A system that has reached its limiting set is said to be at **equilibrium**.

## Types

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Limit_set&action=edit&section=1)]
- [fixed points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed_point_(mathematics))
- [periodic orbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_orbit)
- [limit cycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limit_cycle)
- [attractors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attractor)

In general, limits sets can be very complicated as in the case of [strange attractors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strange_attractor), but for 2-dimensional dynamical systems the [Poincaré–Bendixson theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9%E2%80%93Bendixson_theorem) provides a simple characterization of all nonempty, compact     ω   {\displaystyle \omega }  -limit sets that contain at most finitely many fixed points as a fixed point, a periodic orbit, or a union of fixed points and [homoclinic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homoclinic) or [heteroclinic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heteroclinic) orbits connecting those fixed points.

## Definition for iterated functions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Limit_set&action=edit&section=2)]

Let     X   {\displaystyle X}   be a [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space), and let     f : X → X   {\displaystyle f:X\rightarrow X}   be a [continuous function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_function). The     ω   {\displaystyle \omega }  -limit set of     x ∈ X   {\displaystyle x\in X}  , denoted by     ω ( x , f )   {\displaystyle \omega (x,f)}  , is the set of [cluster points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limit_point) of the [forward orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit_(dynamics))     {  f  n   ( x )  }  n ∈  N      {\displaystyle \{f^{n}(x)\}_{n\in \mathbb {N} }}   of the [iterated function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iterated_function)     f   {\displaystyle f}  .[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limit_set#cite_note-1) Hence,     y ∈ ω ( x , f )   {\displaystyle y\in \omega (x,f)}   [if and only if](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_and_only_if) there is a strictly increasing sequence of natural numbers     {  n  k    }  k ∈  N      {\displaystyle \{n_{k}\}_{k\in \mathbb {N} }}   such that      f   n  k     ( x ) → y   {\displaystyle f^{n_{k}}(x)\rightarrow y}   as     k → ∞   {\displaystyle k\rightarrow \infty }  . Another way to express this is

     ω ( x , f ) =  ⋂  n ∈  N       {  f  k   ( x ) : k > n }  ¯   ,   {\displaystyle \omega (x,f)=\bigcap _{n\in \mathbb {N} }{\overline {\{f^{k}(x):k>n\}}},}

where       S ¯     {\displaystyle {\overline {S}}}   denotes the *closure* of set     S   {\displaystyle S}  . The points in the limit set are non-wandering (but may not be *[recurrent points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrent_point)*). This may also be formulated as the outer limit ([limsup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limsup)) of a sequence of sets, such that

     ω ( x , f ) =  ⋂  n = 1   ∞       ⋃  k = n   ∞   {  f  k   ( x ) }  ¯   .   {\displaystyle \omega (x,f)=\bigcap _{n=1}^{\infty }{\overline {\bigcup _{k=n}^{\infty }\{f^{k}(x)\}}}.}

If     f   {\displaystyle f}   is a [homeomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeomorphism) (that is, a bicontinuous bijection), then the     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }  -limit set is defined in a similar fashion, but for the backward orbit; *i.e.*     α ( x , f ) = ω ( x ,  f  − 1   )   {\displaystyle \alpha (x,f)=\omega (x,f^{-1})}  .

Both sets are     f   {\displaystyle f}  -invariant, and if     X   {\displaystyle X}   is [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space), they are compact and nonempty.

## Definition for flows

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Limit_set&action=edit&section=3)]

Given a [real dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_dynamical_system)     ( T , X , φ )   {\displaystyle (T,X,\varphi )}   with [flow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flow_(mathematics))     φ :  R  × X → X   {\displaystyle \varphi :\mathbb {R} \times X\to X} , a point     x   {\displaystyle x}  , we call a point     y   {\displaystyle y}   an     ω   {\displaystyle \omega }  -**limit point** of *x   {\displaystyle x}* if there exists a sequence     (  t  n    )  n ∈  N      {\displaystyle (t_{n})_{n\in \mathbb {N} }}   in      R    {\displaystyle \mathbb {R} }   so that

      lim  n → ∞    t  n   = ∞   {\displaystyle \lim _{n\to \infty }t_{n}=\infty }        lim  n → ∞   φ (  t  n   , x ) = y   {\displaystyle \lim _{n\to \infty }\varphi (t_{n},x)=y}  .

For an [orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit_(dynamics))     γ   {\displaystyle \gamma }   of     ( T , X , φ )   {\displaystyle (T,X,\varphi )}  , we say that     y   {\displaystyle y}   is an     ω   {\displaystyle \omega }  -**limit point** of     γ   {\displaystyle \gamma }  , if it is an     ω   {\displaystyle \omega }  -**limit point** of some point on the orbit.

Analogously we call *y   {\displaystyle y}* an     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }  -**limit point** of *x   {\displaystyle x}* if there exists a sequence     (  t  n    )  n ∈  N      {\displaystyle (t_{n})_{n\in \mathbb {N} }}   in      R    {\displaystyle \mathbb {R} }   so that

      lim  n → ∞    t  n   = − ∞   {\displaystyle \lim _{n\to \infty }t_{n}=-\infty }        lim  n → ∞   φ (  t  n   , x ) = y   {\displaystyle \lim _{n\to \infty }\varphi (t_{n},x)=y}  .

For an [orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit_(dynamics))     γ   {\displaystyle \gamma }   of     ( T , X , φ )   {\displaystyle (T,X,\varphi )}  , we say that *y   {\displaystyle y}* is an     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }  -**limit point** of     γ   {\displaystyle \gamma }  , if it is an     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }  -**limit point** of some point on the orbit.

The set of all     ω   {\displaystyle \omega }  -limit points (    α   {\displaystyle \alpha }  -limit points) for a given orbit     γ   {\displaystyle \gamma }   is called     ω   {\displaystyle \omega }  -**limit set** (    α   {\displaystyle \alpha }  -**limit set**) for     γ   {\displaystyle \gamma }   and denoted      lim  ω   γ   {\displaystyle \lim _{\omega }\gamma }   (     lim  α   γ   {\displaystyle \lim _{\alpha }\gamma }  ).

If the     ω   {\displaystyle \omega }  -limit set (    α   {\displaystyle \alpha }  -limit set) is disjoint from the orbit     γ   {\displaystyle \gamma }  , that is      lim  ω   γ ∩ γ = ∅   {\displaystyle \lim _{\omega }\gamma \cap \gamma =\varnothing }   (     lim  α   γ ∩ γ = ∅   {\displaystyle \lim _{\alpha }\gamma \cap \gamma =\varnothing }  ), we call      lim  ω   γ   {\displaystyle \lim _{\omega }\gamma }   (     lim  α   γ   {\displaystyle \lim _{\alpha }\gamma }  ) a **[ω-limit cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%CE%A9-limit_cycle)** (**[α-limit cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%CE%91-limit_cycle)**).

Alternatively the limit sets can be defined as

      lim  ω   γ :=  ⋂  s ∈  R       { φ ( x , t ) : t > s }  ¯     {\displaystyle \lim _{\omega }\gamma :=\bigcap _{s\in \mathbb {R} }{\overline {\{\varphi (x,t):t>s\}}}}

and

      lim  α   γ :=  ⋂  s ∈  R       { φ ( x , t ) : t < s }  ¯   .   {\displaystyle \lim _{\alpha }\gamma :=\bigcap _{s\in \mathbb {R} }{\overline {\{\varphi (x,t):t<s\}}}.}

### Examples

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Limit_set&action=edit&section=4)]
- For any [periodic orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_orbit)     γ   {\displaystyle \gamma }   of a dynamical system,      lim  ω   γ =  lim  α   γ = γ   {\displaystyle \lim _{\omega }\gamma =\lim _{\alpha }\gamma =\gamma }
- For any [fixed point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed_point_(mathematics))      x  0     {\displaystyle x_{0}}   of a dynamical system,      lim  ω    x  0   =  lim  α    x  0   =  x  0     {\displaystyle \lim _{\omega }x_{0}=\lim _{\alpha }x_{0}=x_{0}}

### Properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Limit_set&action=edit&section=5)]
- lim  ω   γ   {\displaystyle \lim _{\omega }\gamma }   and      lim  α   γ   {\displaystyle \lim _{\alpha }\gamma }   are [closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_set)
- if     X   {\displaystyle X}   is compact then      lim  ω   γ   {\displaystyle \lim _{\omega }\gamma }   and      lim  α   γ   {\displaystyle \lim _{\alpha }\gamma }   are [nonempty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonempty), [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_set) and [connected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connected_space)
- lim  ω   γ   {\displaystyle \lim _{\omega }\gamma }   and      lim  α   γ   {\displaystyle \lim _{\alpha }\gamma }   are     φ   {\displaystyle \varphi }  -invariant, that is     φ (  R  ×  lim  ω   γ ) =  lim  ω   γ   {\displaystyle \varphi (\mathbb {R} \times \lim _{\omega }\gamma )=\lim _{\omega }\gamma }   and     φ (  R  ×  lim  α   γ ) =  lim  α   γ   {\displaystyle \varphi (\mathbb {R} \times \lim _{\alpha }\gamma )=\lim _{\alpha }\gamma }

Limit set

# Limit set

 [Edit links](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q1825444#sitelinks-wikipedia)                          From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia   State of a dynamic system after an infinitely long time This article is about the notion of a limit set in the area of dynamical systems. For the notion of a limit in set theory, see [Set-theoretic limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set-theoretic_limit). In [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), especially in the study of [dynamical systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamical_system), a **limit set** is the state a dynamical system reaches after an infinite amount of time has passed, by either going forward or backwards in time. Limit sets are important because they can be used to understand the long term behavior of a dynamical system. A system that has reached its limiting set is said to be at **equilibrium**.

Types

# Types

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Limit_set&action=edit&section=1)]
- [fixed points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed_point_(mathematics))
- [periodic orbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_orbit)
- [limit cycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limit_cycle)
- [attractors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attractor)

In general, limits sets can be very complicated as in the case of [strange attractors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strange_attractor), but for 2-dimensional dynamical systems the [Poincaré–Bendixson theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9%E2%80%93Bendixson_theorem) provides a simple characterization of all nonempty, compact     ω   {\displaystyle \omega }  -limit sets that contain at most finitely many fixed points as a fixed point, a periodic orbit, or a union of fixed points and [homoclinic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homoclinic) or [heteroclinic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heteroclinic) orbits connecting those fixed points.

Definition for iterated functions

# Definition for iterated functions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Limit_set&action=edit&section=2)]

Let     X   {\displaystyle X}   be a [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space), and let     f : X → X   {\displaystyle f:X\rightarrow X}   be a [continuous function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_function). The     ω   {\displaystyle \omega }  -limit set of     x ∈ X   {\displaystyle x\in X}  , denoted by     ω ( x , f )   {\displaystyle \omega (x,f)}  , is the set of [cluster points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limit_point) of the [forward orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit_(dynamics))     {  f  n   ( x )  }  n ∈  N      {\displaystyle \{f^{n}(x)\}_{n\in \mathbb {N} }}   of the [iterated function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iterated_function)     f   {\displaystyle f}  .[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limit_set#cite_note-1) Hence,     y ∈ ω ( x , f )   {\displaystyle y\in \omega (x,f)}   [if and only if](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_and_only_if) there is a strictly increasing sequence of natural numbers     {  n  k    }  k ∈  N      {\displaystyle \{n_{k}\}_{k\in \mathbb {N} }}   such that      f   n  k     ( x ) → y   {\displaystyle f^{n_{k}}(x)\rightarrow y}   as     k → ∞   {\displaystyle k\rightarrow \infty }  . Another way to express this is

     ω ( x , f ) =  ⋂  n ∈  N       {  f  k   ( x ) : k > n }  ¯   ,   {\displaystyle \omega (x,f)=\bigcap _{n\in \mathbb {N} }{\overline {\{f^{k}(x):k>n\}}},}

where       S ¯     {\displaystyle {\overline {S}}}   denotes the *closure* of set     S   {\displaystyle S}  . The points in the limit set are non-wandering (but may not be *[recurrent points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrent_point)*). This may also be formulated as the outer limit ([limsup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limsup)) of a sequence of sets, such that

     ω ( x , f ) =  ⋂  n = 1   ∞       ⋃  k = n   ∞   {  f  k   ( x ) }  ¯   .   {\displaystyle \omega (x,f)=\bigcap _{n=1}^{\infty }{\overline {\bigcup _{k=n}^{\infty }\{f^{k}(x)\}}}.}

If     f   {\displaystyle f}   is a [homeomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeomorphism) (that is, a bicontinuous bijection), then the     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }  -limit set is defined in a similar fashion, but for the backward orbit; *i.e.*     α ( x , f ) = ω ( x ,  f  − 1   )   {\displaystyle \alpha (x,f)=\omega (x,f^{-1})}  .

Both sets are     f   {\displaystyle f}  -invariant, and if     X   {\displaystyle X}   is [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space), they are compact and nonempty.

Definition for flows

# Definition for flows

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Limit_set&action=edit&section=3)]

Given a [real dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_dynamical_system)     ( T , X , φ )   {\displaystyle (T,X,\varphi )}   with [flow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flow_(mathematics))     φ :  R  × X → X   {\displaystyle \varphi :\mathbb {R} \times X\to X} , a point     x   {\displaystyle x}  , we call a point     y   {\displaystyle y}   an     ω   {\displaystyle \omega }  -**limit point** of *x   {\displaystyle x}* if there exists a sequence     (  t  n    )  n ∈  N      {\displaystyle (t_{n})_{n\in \mathbb {N} }}   in      R    {\displaystyle \mathbb {R} }   so that

      lim  n → ∞    t  n   = ∞   {\displaystyle \lim _{n\to \infty }t_{n}=\infty }        lim  n → ∞   φ (  t  n   , x ) = y   {\displaystyle \lim _{n\to \infty }\varphi (t_{n},x)=y}  .

For an [orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit_(dynamics))     γ   {\displaystyle \gamma }   of     ( T , X , φ )   {\displaystyle (T,X,\varphi )}  , we say that     y   {\displaystyle y}   is an     ω   {\displaystyle \omega }  -**limit point** of     γ   {\displaystyle \gamma }  , if it is an     ω   {\displaystyle \omega }  -**limit point** of some point on the orbit.

Analogously we call *y   {\displaystyle y}* an     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }  -**limit point** of *x   {\displaystyle x}* if there exists a sequence     (  t  n    )  n ∈  N      {\displaystyle (t_{n})_{n\in \mathbb {N} }}   in      R    {\displaystyle \mathbb {R} }   so that

      lim  n → ∞    t  n   = − ∞   {\displaystyle \lim _{n\to \infty }t_{n}=-\infty }        lim  n → ∞   φ (  t  n   , x ) = y   {\displaystyle \lim _{n\to \infty }\varphi (t_{n},x)=y}  .

For an [orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit_(dynamics))     γ   {\displaystyle \gamma }   of     ( T , X , φ )   {\displaystyle (T,X,\varphi )}  , we say that *y   {\displaystyle y}* is an     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }  -**limit point** of     γ   {\displaystyle \gamma }  , if it is an     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }  -**limit point** of some point on the orbit.

The set of all     ω   {\displaystyle \omega }  -limit points (    α   {\displaystyle \alpha }  -limit points) for a given orbit     γ   {\displaystyle \gamma }   is called     ω   {\displaystyle \omega }  -**limit set** (    α   {\displaystyle \alpha }  -**limit set**) for     γ   {\displaystyle \gamma }   and denoted      lim  ω   γ   {\displaystyle \lim _{\omega }\gamma }   (     lim  α   γ   {\displaystyle \lim _{\alpha }\gamma }  ).

If the     ω   {\displaystyle \omega }  -limit set (    α   {\displaystyle \alpha }  -limit set) is disjoint from the orbit     γ   {\displaystyle \gamma }  , that is      lim  ω   γ ∩ γ = ∅   {\displaystyle \lim _{\omega }\gamma \cap \gamma =\varnothing }   (     lim  α   γ ∩ γ = ∅   {\displaystyle \lim _{\alpha }\gamma \cap \gamma =\varnothing }  ), we call      lim  ω   γ   {\displaystyle \lim _{\omega }\gamma }   (     lim  α   γ   {\displaystyle \lim _{\alpha }\gamma }  ) a **[ω-limit cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%CE%A9-limit_cycle)** (**[α-limit cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%CE%91-limit_cycle)**).

Alternatively the limit sets can be defined as

      lim  ω   γ :=  ⋂  s ∈  R       { φ ( x , t ) : t > s }  ¯     {\displaystyle \lim _{\omega }\gamma :=\bigcap _{s\in \mathbb {R} }{\overline {\{\varphi (x,t):t>s\}}}}

and

      lim  α   γ :=  ⋂  s ∈  R       { φ ( x , t ) : t < s }  ¯   .   {\displaystyle \lim _{\alpha }\gamma :=\bigcap _{s\in \mathbb {R} }{\overline {\{\varphi (x,t):t<s\}}}.}
